title: The Trough Is Not a Castle · action rehearsal
description: Unassigned 2-minute staging sample from Don Quixote I.3. Two characters, one local dialogue choice, fixed source events. Generic costumes and mimed props; not a replacement for the assigned chapter 1 episode.
script:
story 2
label opening
scene courtyard
show Quixote determined left
show Carrier neutral right
camera wide
I: Night at a roadside inn in La Mancha. I watch from the doorway as Don Quixote guards his armour on a watering trough. He believes this is a knight's vigil in a castle.
Carrier [confused, question]: I only want to water the animals. Why is the trough wearing a helmet?
choice aside
option practical "Whisper: Perhaps the armour could guard a different corner?" -> practical
option theatrical "Whisper: Your castle appears to have a plumbing problem." -> theatrical
label practical
Quixote [determined, insist]: Honour does not move aside for a thirsty mule.
goto encounter
label theatrical
Quixote [skeptical, question]: A castle has many trials. Apparently yours is vocabulary.
goto encounter
label encounter
scene courtyard
show Quixote determined left
show Carrier confused right
camera wide
I: The carrier ignores the warning and moves the armour. To him, it is an obstruction. To Quixote, it is an outrage.
act Quixote attack Carrier "Quixote strikes the carrier with his lance. The man is badly hurt; Quixote returns to guarding the armour."
move Carrier exit
I: Another carrier later approaches the trough and is also struck. Their companions throw stones; Quixote shields himself while the innkeeper intervenes.
act Quixote cower "Quixote shelters behind his shield as stones fly from the carriers' companions."
I: The innkeeper hurries through a makeshift knighting ceremony to end the danger. Quixote takes the ceremony seriously and rides away grateful.
act Quixote bow "Quixote gives a ceremonious bow before leaving the inn."
I: From the doorway, I have seen one event interpreted as two different stories: an ordinary task at an inn, and an imagined test of chivalry.
end

Quixote.name: Don Quixote
Quixote.provenance: Fictional manga interpretation of Cervantes's Don Quixote, using shared cartoon-v1 components. Angular face and grey beard suggest the spare, nearly fifty-year-old gentleman of I.1. Generic brown preparation clothes, not a claim of exact Spanish costume reconstruction; armor rests offstage. No real-person likeness.

Carrier.name: The carrier
Carrier.provenance: Fictional unnamed carrier from Don Quixote I.3. Generic rehearsal costume; no real-person likeness.

quiz.prompt: Why does the carrier move the armour?
options: To challenge a knight to a formal duel.
To help with a knighting ceremony.
quiz.explanation: The trough has a practical use. The carrier’s ordinary purpose conflicts with Quixote’s imagined vigil.

quiz.prompt: What turns an ordinary action into an insult in Quixote’s eyes?
options: The carrier announces himself as a knight.
Quixote interprets the event through the conventions of chivalry.
The inn is actually a castle.
quiz.explanation: The mismatch comes from interpretation. Quixote treats the inn as a castle and his armour as part of a sacred vigil.

quiz.prompt: Why does the innkeeper hurry the knighting ceremony?
options: He wants to end the danger caused by his guest.
The carrier asks to become a knight.
He has discovered a real castle.
quiz.explanation: The violence prompts the innkeeper to bring the vigil to an end with a makeshift ceremony.

quiz.prompt: Which part of this adaptation is invented rather than a source event?
options: Quixote guards armour on a trough.
The innkeeper conducts a makeshift ceremony.
The student whispers about a plumbing problem.
quiz.explanation: The student and optional remarks are invented. Both remarks return to the same source event; neither changes Cervantes’s plot.

sources: Cervantes, Don Quixote Part I chapter 3, John Ormsby translation, public domain. Read 2026-10-13: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/996/996-h/996-h.htm#ch3 . The first carrier moves armour to water his animals; Quixote strikes him with a lance. A second carrier is injured, companions throw stones, and the innkeeper hastens a makeshift knighting ceremony. No student intervention changes those events.

All dialogue and the student witness are adapted/invented, not quotations. A generic daytime courtyard stands in for the night-time inn; costumes and unrendered props are rehearsal abstractions. Violence is conveyed without graphic injury. This is a short framework example, not an assigned complete episode or an expansion of the current chapter 1 assignment.
